paras: The expulsion of Abner Debleu from Chinook took place on July 31, 1903, when residents of Chinook, a small river town reached by steamer from Astoria, Oregon, ordered Debleu, a Black man, to leave over what they called his laziness. After weighing whether to lynch him or tar and feather him, they paid $2.75 to have him shipped to Astoria, where police jailed him and then put him aboard a boat for Portland. The Morning Astorian followed the case in three mocking items and reported that Debleu soon returned to Chinook to show he was not afraid.

According to the Astorian, Debleu had made Pacific County, Washington, his headquarters for many years and was said to be past forty, though youthful in appearance. The paper described him as a member of the "Afro-American race" and said the people of Chinook had offered him work, which he declined. It added that he preferred to "bask in the warm sunshine by day and beg, borrow or steal his food by night," a claim for which it gave no specific instance.

On July 31 the citizens of Chinook decided they had "no room in their clean little town for such a man" and told him to "get." When he refused, the Astorian wrote, it was for about ten minutes "a question whether there would be a lynching or just plain tar and feathers." To avert trouble, the men of the town instead collected $2.75 to send him away. Jack Johnson, who happened to be in town and did not wish "to officiate at a lynching," took him on the steamer Miller to Astoria and turned him over, with the money, to Chief of Police Hallock.

Hallock, who the paper said remembered Debleu from a visit during a regatta years earlier, gave him the choice of leaving the city or going to jail. Debleu at first refused and spent a night and a day in the "city tank" before accepting the $2.75. On the night of August 1 he was escorted to the Portland boat, and an officer stood at the gangplank until it sailed.

Before leaving, Debleu was quoted in dialect as wanting to go back to Chinook to show the townspeople he was not afraid of them. By August 6 he had done so, although Chinook residents had vowed to act if he kept appearing on their streets. He passed through the town without staying long enough to invite "forcible measures of removal." No report of any arrest or official action against the Chinook residents appears in the coverage.

The only coverage found was three short local items in the Morning Astorian on August 1, 2 and 6, 1903, and no report in the Black press was found. Under headlines such as "Shipped to Astoria" and "Mr. Abner Debleu Leaves Town," the paper treated the expulsion as comedy and presented the charge of laziness as fact. It called Debleu "the black contention," a "chocolate colored gentleman" and a "chicken chaser," printed his words in exaggerated dialect, and credited his removal from Astoria to the chief's "good council." Its final item also mocked Chinook as a "puritan little" village guarding "the spotless white shield of their town."

accounts.label: Morning Astorian local reports
accounts.gist: Chinook residents, tired of Debleu's "laziness", ordered him out and weighed lynching or tar and feathers before paying to ship him to Astoria, where police jailed him and sent him on to Portland; he later returned to Chinook.

accounts.label: Debleu's words (as quoted by the Astorian)

framing.detail: Headlines "Shipped to Astoria" and "Mr. Abner Debleu Leaves Town" treat the expulsion as comedy, call him "the black contention" and "chicken chaser", present laziness as his offense and the police removal as "good council".
"Abner Returned to Chinook" keeps the dialect and "chocolate colored gentleman" while mocking Chinook as a "puritan little" village guarding "the spotless white shield of their town".
